doc_summary: A position paper arguing NLU benchmarking is broken and proposing four criteria (validity, reliable annotation, statistical power, bias disincentives), arguing that adversarial filtering does not address these causes and that static IID evaluation can be repaired directly. It stresses that a benchmark must actually measure the intended capability rather than merely be hard for current models.

items.claim: Prefers benchmarks whose scores validly reflect the target capability over benchmarks that are merely hard for current models, because difficulty by adversarial selection does not show that a result reflects the intended behavior.
items.quote: collecting examples on which current models fail is neither necessary nor sufficient to create a useful benchmark.

items.claim: Distrusts evaluation data containing annotation artifacts, since a system can reach strong scores by shortcuts rather than by the intended behaviors; test setups should not be solvable or triggerable by superficial cues.
items.quote: An evaluation dataset should be sufficiently free of annotation artifacts (as in Si et al., 2019; Sugawara et al., 2020b; Niven and Kao, 2019) that a system cannot reach near-human levels of performance by any means other than demonstrating the required language-related behaviors.

items.claim: Prefers naturally-occurring distributions over hand-built ones where viable because they reduce the risk that the benchmark is skewed in ways that omit important phenomena, though acknowledges they are often not viable.
items.quote: It is intuitively appealing to, where possible, build benchmark datasets based on naturally-occurring data distributions. This minimizes our effort in creating benchmarks and minimizes the risk that the benchmark is somehow skewed in a way that omits important phenomena.

items.claim: Distrusts expert-authored test data for broad benchmarks because designers' knowledge of what matters steers examples toward known phenomena, which is relevant to auditor-written scenarios that reflect the designer's expectations about what is being tested.
items.quote: expert authorship generally gives members of the research community direct, fine-grained control over the data on which their systems will be evaluated. Intentionally or unintentionally, this can produce data that is oriented toward linguistic phenomena that are widely studied and widely known to be important to the task at hand.

items.claim: Evidence of validity should predict generalization: a good test is one where improvement carries over to any other reasonable evaluation of the same task and domain.
items.quote: If a benchmark fully meets this challenge, we should expect any clear improvement on the benchmark to translate to similar improvements on any other valid and reasonable evaluation data for the same task and language domain.

items.claim: Prefers broad coverage of the real variation in the target domain over tests built around selected failure cases, because filtering to model failures reduces diversity and eliminates coverage of skills the adversary already handles.
items.quote: it can systematically eliminate coverage of linguistic phenomena or skills that are necessary for the task but already well-solved by the adversary model. This mode-seeking (as opposed to mass covering) behavior by adversarial filtering, if left unchecked, tends to reduce dataset diversity and thus make validity harder to achieve.

items.claim: Use small interventions in the data-creation process that remove overused patterns, without constraining creator freedom, to improve data quality while keeping creativity and naturalness.
items.quote: They show that it is possible to significantly improve data quality issues by making small interventions during the crowdsourcing process—like offering additional bonus payments for examples that avoid overused words and constructions—without significantly limiting annotators’ freedom to independently construct creative examples.

items.claim: Crowdsourced examples under standard practice skew toward repetitive, easy cases, so careful piloting and expert augmentation are needed to fill coverage gaps.
items.quote: Existing datasets focus heavily on repetitive, easy cases and often fail to isolate key behaviors (Jia and Liang, 2017; Tsuchiya, 2018; McCoy et al., 2019).

items.claim: Do careful planning and pilot work before large-scale data collection to resolve ambiguity in task guidelines.
items.quote: Careful planning and pilot work before data collection can largely resolve the issue of ambiguous annotation guidelines.

items.claim: Prefers running auxiliary targeted metrics in parallel with the primary test over relying on a single metric to capture everything, because no single dataset can guarantee it never rewards harmful behavior.
items.quote: Rather than trying to fully mitigate bias within a single general dataset and metric for some task, benchmark creators can introduce a family of additional expert-constructed test datasets and metrics that each isolate and measure a specific type of bias.

items.claim: Open problems: how to integrate expert effort into crowdsourced data collection and how to institutionalize use of bias metrics.
items.quote: it is still unclear how best to integrate expert effort into crowdsourced data collection, and we do not yet see a clear institutional model by which to ensure that bias metrics are built and used when they are most needed.
